You can just do avg gas per block * blocks per year / 200 yourself (assuming worst case contract code filling blocks) I've said this in <#847906692183359568> We will veto hardcoding the gas limit if it's brought up on ACD. Is this the most effective way to bloat state though? Is it more damaging to create lots of small contracts instead (per gas)? IIUC, creating a new contract has more "stuff" (in terms of data that needs to be stored) than creating a few very large contracts. I think it's worth stating - you don't have a veto to use. Firstly because that's not how the governance works - the aim is consensus, not necessarily unanimous agreement. If having one objection was enough to block a decision nothing would ever happen. Secondly on this particular issue if the Geth team decided to add a limit that on its own would be enough for the limit to be effectively applied via a soft fork even if Erigon never implemented it. I get that you have a difference of opinion on this but resorting to bullying tactics by threatening to veto is an incredibly unhelpful and unprofessional approach. You are not even working on the mainnet yourself so it's funny to hear this from you. That aside, when we see proposals like this hastily made up hysterically, we will have to say no. If the second most used client's opinion (excluding OE) doesn't count, then I don't know what does. We might as well have governance by geth / EF fiat in that case My main focus may be teku these days but I’m still a besu contributor so I have as much right to speak up as you. I’m not saying a proposal is ready to go to all core devs at this point or that it would be agreed to if it did. I’m simply calling out your unhelpful attitude and making clear that you are seriously overplaying your hand. You don’t have a veto so stop acting like you do. The proposal as a whole runs counter to our thinking, so it's not 'unhelpful attitude' but a fair warning that we are very likely to say no matter if it's sugar coated or not. Gas limit should not be hardcoded period Might be worth formalising what "consensus" here means. That is an entire topic on its own that has, previously, intentionally been left vague. Yup, but it might be worth formalising now, just a thought It is (I believe) intentionally not formalized. It is incredibly difficult to capture an informal system of governance compared to a formal system of governance. Formalizing it gives people a clear attack vector, while informal governance means that anytime someone tries to capture it the "rules" can change (because they were never defined). Like picking up water vs picking up a rock. The water will just reform over your hand if you try to carry it away, while the rock will rigidly stay in its original shape which makes it easier to carry away. Of course, this same property makes it incredibly hard to actually get anything done. 😖 Often we *do* want to "move the water", and this is very hard without a formal system of governance. Can you please define what you mean by "capture" here? Meaning someone or some group, other than the intended person/group, seizes control of the power that the system of governance wields. In this case, the "intended person/group" is "all of the people who make up the Ethereum ecosystem" ideally, though I'm certain we don't currently hit that ideal we do our best to get *close* to that. Intended group is vaguely defined here too :) one person one vote or one ETH one vote? And do all clients intend to hit the same group you do? In-protocol the last level of defence is hard fork which is plutocratic, but teams like geth have explicitly rejected the notion of listening to a plutocratic system. Does that count as a client team capturing the system away from intended group? I think the idea is that right now, there is no "system" to capture away. If it would be formalized as "coredevs have rights to x, this group has rights to c, miners have rights to freely set the gas limit", then one of these groups could go rogue and fend off every attack with "well we all decided that i have right to decide upon this particular issue and you have no say here" Correct, everything is ill-defined on purpose. It is very hard to attack an ill defined system of governance. It definitely has extreme trade-offs in terms of ability to do useful work though, this is a known and very much not-obviously-right trade. I'm not sure if "attack" is the correct framing for this, considering we're all insiders who have our own (mostly) long-term vision for what we'd like to see in ethereum. Also can argue that poorly defining people's powers just obscures where the real power lies, it doesn't remove it "attack" "capture" "rogue" seem to imply well-defined ingroup/outgroup dynamics which don't exist Yep, the power still exists but it is obscured, and from everyone in this case. 🙂 I have my suspicions that the Geth team has quite a bit of power, but I'm not actually certain about that because it isn't formalized and it hasn't been extensively tested, and testing it is extremely difficult/expensive. I suspect even the Geth team doesn't know how much power they *actually* have. I also may have some power (or I may have none), but I don't know how much and if I try to exercise more power than I have I could end up losing power. This causes me to behave in a much more conservative way than if I knew exactly what my limits were. If I was King of Ethereum I would do many things differently. Maybe I *am* King of Ethereum (and I just don't know it due to power obfuscation), but I behave as though I am not, which I would argue is how we *want* the King of Ethereum to behave. 🙂 Interesting point. So if everyone underestimates or chooses not to use the power they have, changes that could otherwise be forced through would now stall. So more bias in favour of ossification? Is that desirable? when governance channel? Also in that case isn't calling it a "veto" helpful? "unless geth or someone else wants to significantly test and exert their power, we as erigon don't want to entertain this kind of change, so it's effectively a veto even if not a formal veto" (cuz erigon clearly *wants* to exert their power on gaslimit matter) Yes, definitely. This is the big downside to this strategy. Bitcoin followed a similar strategy I believe it is a big part of the reason why they *did* ossify. That is a serious risk for Ethereum too long term I think! I used to also think it was a veto, but it is a Schrodinger veto. 🙂 We don't know whether Erigon has veto power over this particular subject until after they try to exercise it. Until then, they both have and do not have veto power. 😄 Even then, it is fuzzy. They may have "veto" power if it turns out the community is "meh" on the topic, or they don't have veto power if the community is strongly in favor of the topic. You could, perhaps, consider "the community" as the universal waveform that collapses into an observable state only after it is observed... or something. 😛 Interesting viewpoint. Might be worth writing an article :) Discord chat will get lost I did. 🙂 https://medium.com/coinmonks/how-ethereum-governance-works-71856426b63a Not exactly what we discussed here, but very related. Have read this :) But yeah on why you're against formalising, what underplaying power means etc In-protocol voting etc I think the only party qualified to set the gas limit are node owners, as they inherently know best what are actual limits, as a group. Not devs that are only trying to imagine the utility function of actual node owners. It's very hard to make a sybil-resistant system for this under PoW, but under PoS node owners = stakers. In addition, right now gas limit is so low it decreases number of active nodes. Empirically, I turned off my ethereum node as I stopped needing it as new apps moved elsewhere. Instead I set up a matic node. I know of one person that also turned off their ethereum node for the same reason. I have turned off my Ethereum node on a number of occasions because it was too hard/expensive to run. Only reason I keep turning it back on is because I do core dev adjacent work that requires me to run a node so I went out and finally bought more hardware for it. Essentially, I run it "as part of my job", not as an end user. That being said, the big problem here is that not everyone is working toward the same goal. A node operator may only care about the 6-month utility of Ethereum. People also don't agree on the probability/impact of stat actors coming after Ethereum. how is it too expensive too run? do you use a raspberry pi? serious question. the cost to run it is a rounding error to me. it was just a constant effort in keeping it updated and all that. I can see the argument that it *would* be too expensive to run if it stops being able to run on a laptop or pc, or at least requires raid. Disk space is the big one. Until recently I just had a normal 1TB drive that was full of other stuff (games, movies, etc.) I didn't have enough space leftover for several hundred GBs of Ethereum. It wasn't a cost issue so much as I was trying to run Ethereum on the computer I bought for day-to-day tasks. I didn't (until recently) go out of my way to buy specialized hardware just to run an Ethereum client. I also have a client running on a cloud server where SSD disk space is a bit of a premium. The host has 2x 240GB drive IIRC, which makes for a pretty tight experience when you also are running a Bitcoin client, a Monero client, a few web apps, an IPFS server, etc. (currently strategy is to pave the Ethereum client every few months and sync from scratch using snap/fast/warp sync) It's not clear to me that node owners will be stakers on pos. I don't know the numbers but I'd expect to be many more execution clients running than beacon nodes as the former have many more applications. the cost of a 4 tb ssd should be viewed relatively to fees. during the demand peaks 3 uniswap swaps pay for a 4 tb ssd. And of course it's not comparable: even if you turn off your node, you still have your ssd. This is why increasing the gas limit increases the number of nodes: cost of additional hardware is currently a rounding error for a power user/dev compared to costs of using ethereum. So increasing hardware costs by a tiny bit while decreasing costs to use ethereum much more and increasing number of users = more nodes Additionally, current geth doesn't support pruning old blocks. The actual limit should be state size, not old blocks. State is about 50GB iirc? that's true, but it's probably the best sybil-resistant sampling that can exist. itch I cannot scratch what is the point of running Ethereum node, when you cannot use the network because of abhorrent fees? Yes, this is exactly my point. it's like one of those ridiculous art exercises like "full validation just because" or "we must preserve history at all costs" of course linear scaling has limits: people should be able to run nodes on consumer hardware in their homes. But current parameters are set for *raspberry pi* nodes. I find that ridiculous. I see it as a form of expression that runs counter to simple pragmatism Ryzen 5950x or Threadrippers are consumer hardware too FWIW but if the network demands that users build PCs with Threadrippers, so be it otherwise, they will burn more on fees anyway that's a valid node point too, although at this point we are talking about 1B+ gas limits (assuming some parallel processing), like what bch is doing with their ethereum clone (moeingevm). 100M gas limit could run on an average pc or slightly above average laptop. Binance is a fork of Geth, we won't know its true

I think it's worth stating - you don't have a veto to use. Firstly because that's not how the governance works - the aim is consensus, not necessarily unanimous agreement. If having one objection was enough to block a decision nothing would ever happen.

I think the only party qualified to set the gas limit are node owners, as they inherently know best what are actual limits, as a group. we don't "don't store intermediate stuff"
